Downvotes should be reserved for posts that break the rules. It pains me to see legitimate posts downvoted into oblivion because voters disagree with them or are butthurt. I do think, however, that a post's score should reflect if voters dislike the post, even if it does not break the rules. I propose one possible solution:

I propose adding a panel of with legitimate reasons for downvoting. The user must select at least one reason, or the full -1 downvote will not be applied, and it will be considered a lessor downvote (explained below). Basically, one click on the downvote button would be a typical/lessor downvote, and a second click would bring up a "reasons for downvoting" panel, and a third click would clear the downvote.

The -1 downvote panel would have a list of reasons for downvoting (ex, Breaks the rules, spam), or for threads, also (misleading title, improperly sourced). There is a possibility of having the user would have to provide written justification in some cases. The -1 downvotes would be moderated somehow, and it would be possible to revoke a user's privileges for abusing the -1 downvotes. I know this means more work, but I feel strongly for free speech. I would be willing to moderate.

As for the lessor downvotes, no justification would be required. I propose that ~five lessor downvotes would result in a single -1 vote applied to the post. This way more than 80% (>5/6 to be exact) of the voters would have to downvote a post for it to be in negative territory. This allows users to downvote a post if there is a strong consensus is that it should be downvoted.

I propose the number five because this allows a minority of upvoters to outvote the downvoters. I think this is a good thing because:

  • if a few people believe a rule abiding post should be heard, they should not be silenced, even if the post is racist or unsettling.

  • The number is high to be in favor of upvotes, since if a post truly should be downvoted, the rules will already cover it, and a -1 vote can be applied. A -1 downvote should be a serious mark. Again, I don't think a post should be downvoted unless there is a very strong consensus. Also:

  • Populatirty is primarily determined by the number of upvotes a post has, not by downvotes. In time, "bad" posts will not garner enough upvotes to be visible anyway.

  • This prevents posts from being hidden due to an initial wave of downvotes (since you need five votes before a -1 is applied). It also makes voting manipulation more difficult.

Okay, I posted something like this earlier, but Voat blew up before I could post it. Here it is again:

What you want to do is answer the question: "What is the probability that I would observe a correlation as extreme as the one I observed given that my alternative hypothesis (in this case, correlation < 0) is false?" In this case, we measure the probability from positive infinity as the p-value and the extremeness is how negative the correlation is.

In this case, we will use correlation = p = 0 as our reference, since it is the closest value to our criteria (p<0) that does not fit our criteria.

How this works: If you sample data from an independent, identically-distributed normal distribution (aka iid normal), then you can take the sample correlation (r) and transform it to a value that ranges from -infinity to infinity. This is simply arctanh(r) (hyperbolic arctangent). This new variable has a distribution of Normal(p, 1/sqrt(n-3)), where n is the sample size, and 1/sqrt(n-3) is the standard deviation of the distribution. Note that regardless of the actual correlation, the standard deviation of the correlation only depends on the sample size.

What one usually does is standardize the transformed variable to Z, where Z = sqrt(n-3) * arctanh(r). This value represents where on the Normal(0,1) curve the sample correlation lies when you assume that p = 0.

After looking at this value, you take the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of a normal distribution at that point, which gives you the exact probability that you observe a sample correlation equal to or less than (i.e., "extreme") the one you observed IF p = 0. If that probability is low (<5% is usually considered low), then you "reject the null hypothesis" that p >= 0.

Likewise, you can construct a confidence interval by assuming that p = r, adding +/- CDF(1- alpha/2) to Z, and then transforming those two values back to correlation by using tanh(1/sqrt(n-3) * x), where x = Z +/- CDF(1-alpha/2), and alpha is the "level of confidence that you want". It is divided by two because you have two different sides of the correlation that have equal probabilities. This is effectively a maximum likelihood estimate of an interval of values that the true correlation could be.

Bear in mind that this is not a catch-all test, and more complex data requires more robust treatment in order to construct these tests. For your situation, though, it is perfectly acceptable.

Also note that the derivation for the motivation of the hyperbolic transformation is complicated and is usually taken for granted.
